claims.text: The as-cast high-entropy alloy is homogeneously mixed.
The as-cast alloy lacks significant nanoscale phase segregation.
The as-cast alloy lacks significant local lattice strain.
Moderate thermal annealing induces mild nanoscale phase segregation.
Annealing generates localized lattice strain while preserving overall alloy integrity.
Annealing produces nanoscale compositional fluctuations and increased local strain at grain boundaries and interfaces.
Strain fields created by phase separation locally enhance electron–phonon coupling.
The annealing-induced inhomogeneity increases the density of electronic states favorable for Cooper-pair formation.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling and the associated electronic-state changes enable a superconducting transition below a critical temperature.
Cooper pairing is absent in the more homogeneous as-cast state.
Annealed samples will exhibit a marked drop to zero electrical resistivity at the superconducting transition.
Annealed samples will exhibit an onset of the Meissner effect.
Untreated as-cast samples will remain resistive and lack a Meissner response below the test temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies only when nanoscale inhomogeneity is sufficient to enhance electron–phonon interactions without producing macroscopic defects or deleterious impurity phases.
Any superconductivity produced by the proposed mechanism is likely confined to temperatures below approximately 10 K.

contradictions.description: The baseline definitively states that the untreated alloy has no superconducting response below the test temperature, while the uncertainty field describes superconductivity in this alloy system as uncharacterized. The asserted baseline behavior therefore exceeds the stated state of knowledge.
